hints: Notice the hammer loses all its $10 \text{ J}$ of kinetic energy while the nail moves only $5.0 \text{ mm}$ into the plank.
Connect energy loss to work done against the resistive force: $\text{work done} = \text{average force} \times \text{distance moved}$.
Convert $5.0 \text{ mm}$ to metres in $\text{m}$ before rearranging to $F = W/d$ and check that a very small distance gives a very large force.
walkthrough: The useful data are kinetic energy $W = 10 \text{ J}$ transferred to work pushing the nail, and distance $d = 5.0 \text{ mm} = 0.0050 \text{ m}$.
The governing physics is work done by a force: $W = Fd$, where $F$ is the average force opposing the motion of the nail.
Substitute values with units: $F = 10 \text{ J} / 0.0050 \text{ m} = 2000 \text{ N}$.
The unit check gives $\text{J m}^{-1} = \text{N}$, and the large value is sensible because $10 \text{ J}$ is dissipated over only a few millimetres. This is option D.

options.A: Too small by a factor of 40000. This comes from multiplying $10 \times 0.0050$ instead of dividing work by distance.
options.B: Too small. This comes from dividing $10$ by $5.0$ without converting $5.0 \text{ mm}$ to $0.0050 \text{ m}$.
options.C: Too small by a factor of 40. This may come from a power-of-ten error when converting millimetres to metres.
options.D: Work done $W = Fd$ equals the $10 \text{ J}$ transferred, so $F = 10 / 0.0050 = 2000 \text{ N}$.
